claim: BRCA1 plays a critical role in homology-directed repair (HDR) of DNA double strand breaks.
source: BRCA1 plays a critical role in homology-directed repair (HDR) of DNA double strand breaks, and the repair defect of BRCA1-mutant cancer cells is being targeted with platinum drugs and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about BRCA1's function.

claim: The repair defect of BRCA1-mutant cancer cells is being targeted with platinum drugs and PARP inhibitors.
source: BRCA1 plays a critical role in homology-directed repair (HDR) of DNA double strand breaks, and the repair defect of BRCA1-mutant cancer cells is being targeted with platinum drugs and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a current therapeutic approach.

claim: The BRCA1-PALB2 interaction dictates the choice between HR and SSA.
source: Importantly, our results also demonstrate that the BRCA1-PALB2 interaction dictates the choice between HR and SSA.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Germline, heterozygous mutations in BRCA1 confer high risk of breast and ovarian cancer development in an autosomal dominant fashion.
source: Germline, heterozygous mutations in BRCA1 confer high risk of breast and ovarian cancer development in an autosomal dominant fashion (Couch et al., 2014; Fackenthal and Olopade, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BRCA1 has been implicated in numerous cellular processes including DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, centrosome duplication, and transcriptional regulation.
source: BRCA1 has been implicated in numerous cellular processes including DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, centrosome duplication, and transcriptional regulation, etc. (Deng, 2006; Mullan et al., 2006; Roy et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BRCA1 localizes to discrete nuclear foci and colocalizes with the recombination enzyme RAD51.
source: Ever since BRCA1 was found to localize to discrete nuclear foci and colocalize with the recombination enzyme RAD51 (Scully et al., 1997), its function in homologous recombination (HR)-based repair of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) has been a subject of intense study (Moynahan and Jasin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scully et al., 1997.

claim: Tumors arising from BRCA1 mutation carriers usually show loss of the wild-type allele.
source: Tumors arising from BRCA1 mutation carriers usually show loss of the wild-type (wt) allele, which renders tumor cells biallelically null for the gene.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about BRCA1-associated tumors.

claim: Genome instability resulting from the DNA repair defect following the loss of BRCA1 is a driver of tumor development.
source: It is generally believed that genome instability resulting from the DNA repair defect following the loss of BRCA1 is a driver of tumor development (Li and Greenberg, 2012; Venkitaraman, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The DNA repair defect that leads to tumor development is an 'Achilles' Heel' of tumor cells, which can be selectively killed by platinum drugs and PARP inhibitors.
source: Importantly, the very DNA repair defect that leads to tumor development is also an 'Achilles' Heel' of the resulting tumor cells, which can be selectively killed by suitable DNA-damaging agents that target HR defect, such as platinum drugs and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors (Lord and Ashworth, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lord and Ashworth, 2016.

claim: The human BRCA1 gene consists of 24 exons encoding a large polypeptide of 1863 amino acid residues.
source: The human BRCA1 gene consists of 24 exons encoding a large polypeptide of 1863 amino acid residues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the structure of the BRCA1 gene.

claim: BRCA1 contains a RING domain at the N terminus and a tandem BRCT domain at the C terminus.
source: BRCA1 contains a RING domain at the N terminus and a tandem BRCT domain at the C terminus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two nuclear localization signals (NLSs) facilitate the localization of BRCA1 primarily to the nucleus.
source: Two nuclear localization signals (NLSs) facilitate the localization of BRCA1 primarily to the nucleus (Chen et al., 1996), whereas a nuclear export signal (NES) can mediate its cytoplasmic export (Rodríguez and Henderson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 1996.

claim: A nuclear export signal (NES) can mediate BRCA1's cytoplasmic export.
source: Two nuclear localization signals (NLSs) facilitate the localization of BRCA1 primarily to the nucleus (Chen et al., 1996), whereas a nuclear export signal (NES) can mediate its cytoplasmic export (Rodríguez and Henderson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodríguez and Henderson, 2000.

claim: The RING domain of BRCA1 binds to a similar domain in its close partner BARD1.
source: The RING domain of BRCA1 binds to a similar domain in its close partner BARD1 (Wu et al., 1996), leading to the formation of a stoichiometric complex that possesses substantial ubiquitin E3 ligase activity (Hashizume et al., 2001; Ruffner et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 1996.

claim: The BRCA1-BARD1 complex possesses substantial ubiquitin E3 ligase activity.
source: The RING domain of BRCA1 binds to a similar domain in its close partner BARD1 (Wu et al., 1996), leading to the formation of a stoichiometric complex that possesses substantial ubiquitin E3 ligase activity (Hashizume et al., 2001; Ruffner et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hashizume et al., 2001 and Ruffner et al., 2001.

claim: Binding of BARD1 to BRCA1 shields the NES and helps retain BRCA1 in the nucleus.
source: At the same time, binding of BARD1 to BRCA1 shields the NES and helps retain BRCA1 in the nucleus (Fabbro et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fabbro et al., 2002.

claim: The BRCT domain directly binds, in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, to BRIP1, CtIP and Abraxas.
source: The BRCT domain directly binds, in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, to at least three other proteins, namely BRIP1, CtIP and Abraxas, all of which have function in DNA repair (Huen et al., 2010; Jiang and Greenberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huen et al., 2010 and Jiang and Greenberg, 2015.

claim: BRIP1, CtIP and Abraxas all have function in DNA repair.
source: The BRCT domain directly binds, in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, to at least three other proteins, namely BRIP1, CtIP and Abraxas, all of which have function in DNA repair (Huen et al., 2010; Jiang and Greenberg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huen et al., 2010 and Jiang and Greenberg, 2015.

claim: BRCA1 contains a highly conserved coiled-coil (CC) motif that directly binds PALB2.
source: Additionally, BRCA1 contains a highly conserved coiled-coil (CC) motif that directly binds PALB2, the partner and localizer of BRCA2 (Xia et al., 2006), which links BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the HR pathway (Sy et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xia et al., 2006.

claim: PALB2 is the partner and localizer of BRCA2.
source: Additionally, BRCA1 contains a highly conserved coiled-coil (CC) motif that directly binds PALB2, the partner and localizer of BRCA2 (Xia et al., 2006), which links BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the HR pathway (Sy et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xia et al., 2006.

claim: PALB2 links BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the HR pathway.
source: Additionally, BRCA1 contains a highly conserved coiled-coil (CC) motif that directly binds PALB2, the partner and localizer of BRCA2 (Xia et al., 2006), which links BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the HR pathway (Sy et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sy et al., 2009 and Zhang et al., 2009a, 2009b.

claim: The BIC database contains a total of 15,311 entries of BRCA1 sequence alterations.
source: It contains a total of 15,311 entries of BRCA1 sequence alterations, among which 6133 (40%) are frameshift or protein-truncating mutations, which can generally be classified as pathogenic.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the BIC database content.

claim: 6133 (40%) of BRCA1 sequence alterations in the BIC database are frameshift or protein-truncating mutations, which can generally be classified as pathogenic.
source: It contains a total of 15,311 entries of BRCA1 sequence alterations, among which 6133 (40%) are frameshift or protein-truncating mutations, which can generally be classified as pathogenic.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the BIC database content and classification.

claim: 4577 (30%) of BRCA1 sequence alterations in the BIC database are missense variants, most of which are considered to be of 'unknown clinical importance'.
source: Importantly, 4577 (30%) are missense variants, most of which are considered to be of 'unknown clinical importance', or commonly known as variants of unknown (or uncertain) clinical significance (VUSs), the interpretation of which remains a challenge (Couch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the BIC database content and the challenge of VUS interpretation.

claim: The interpretation of variants of unknown clinical significance (VUSs) remains a challenge.
source: Importantly, 4577 (30%) are missense variants, most of which are considered to be of 'unknown clinical importance', or commonly known as variants of unknown (or uncertain) clinical significance (VUSs), the interpretation of which remains a challenge (Couch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Couch et al., 2014.

claim: C61G and C64R mutations disrupt BARD1 binding.
source: The list included 11 variants with known or partially known functional consequences: two in the RING domain (C61G and C64R) that disrupt BARD1 binding, three in the CC motif (M1400V, L1407P and M1411T) that affect PALB2 binding and six in the BRCT domain (S1655F, C1697R, R1699Q, A1708E, S1715R and M1775R) that abrogate BRCA1 interaction with Abraxas, BRIP1 and CtIP (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: M1400V, L1407P and M1411T mutations affect PALB2 binding.
source: The list included 11 variants with known or partially known functional consequences: two in the RING domain (C61G and C64R) that disrupt BARD1 binding, three in the CC motif (M1400V, L1407P and M1411T) that affect PALB2 binding and six in the BRCT domain (S1655F, C1697R, R1699Q, A1708E, S1715R and M1775R) that abrogate BRCA1 interaction with Abraxas, BRIP1 and CtIP (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: S1655F, C1697R, R1699Q, A1708E, S1715R and M1775R mutations abrogate BRCA1 interaction with Abraxas, BRIP1 and CtIP.
source: The list included 11 variants with known or partially known functional consequences: two in the RING domain (C61G and C64R) that disrupt BARD1 binding, three in the CC motif (M1400V, L1407P and M1411T) that affect PALB2 binding and six in the BRCT domain (S1655F, C1697R, R1699Q, A1708E, S1715R and M1775R) that abrogate BRCA1 interaction with Abraxas, BRIP1 and CtIP (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: P871L, E1038G, K1183R and S1613G are present in 'wild-type' BRCA1 cDNAs from multiple independent sources.
source: Notably, our sequencing analysis revealed P871L, E1038G, K1183R and S1613G in the 'wild-type' BRCA1 cDNAs from multiple independent sources.
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis performed in this study.

claim: P871L, E1038G, K1183R and S1613G are considered as neutral/benign by both BIC and ClinVar.
source: Indeed, they are considered as neutral/benign by both BIC and ClinVar.
evidence: This is stated based on database classifications.

claim: C61G and A1708E are considered pathogenic by ClinVar.
source: Among the rest of the top 22 variants in ClinVar, C61G and A1708E are considered pathogenic, and the rest are all considered benign largely based on genetic or epidemiological evidence.
evidence: This is stated based on ClinVar database classification.

claim: C61G and C64R reduced BRCA1 HR activity by ~5-fold to a level slightly above the vector control.
source: Under the setting used, C61G and C64R reduced BRCA1 HR activity by ~5-fold to a level slightly above the vector control (Figure 1D and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 2.

claim: L1407P and M1411T mutations reduced HR by ~4.5-fold.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Sy et al., 2009), variants L1407P and M1411T, which abrogate or substantially impair PALB2 binding, reduced HR by ~4.5-fold, whereas M1400V, which moderately impairs PALB2 binding (Figure 1B, lane 15), caused a ~ 25% decrease in the apparent HR activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and consistent with a previous report cited as Sy et al., 2009.

claim: M1400V caused a ~25% decrease in the apparent HR activity.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Sy et al., 2009), variants L1407P and M1411T, which abrogate or substantially impair PALB2 binding, reduced HR by ~4.5-fold, whereas M1400V, which moderately impairs PALB2 binding (Figure 1B, lane 15), caused a ~ 25% decrease in the apparent HR activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All variants that are neutral for protein-protein interaction at the RING, coiled-coil and BRCT domains showed greater than 85% of the HR activity of the wt protein.
source: In contrast, all variants that are neutral for protein-protein interaction at the RING, coiled-coil and BRCT domains showed greater than 85% of the HR activity of the wt protein.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the HR assay.

claim: The cutoff threshold of the HR assay was calculated to be 54.3–54.7%.
source: Using variants that have been functionally characterized previously as controls, our assay was found to be both sensitive and specific, and the cutoff threshold of the assay was calculated to be 54.3–54.7%, which would define M1400V and all the protein-protein interaction neutral variants as being functionally benign.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the assay data.

claim: Depletion of BRCA1 in human cells resulted in a reduction of the basal SSA activity.
source: Consistent with a previous report that Brca1-deficient mouse cells show reduced SSA (Stark et al., 2004), depletion of BRCA1 in the human cells resulted in a reduction of the (already low) basal SSA activity (Figure 2A), and re-expression of wt BRCA1 restored the SSA activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with a previous report cited as Stark et al., 2004.

claim: Re-expression of wt BRCA1 restored the SSA activity.
source: Consistent with a previous report that Brca1-deficient mouse cells show reduced SSA (Stark et al., 2004), depletion of BRCA1 in the human cells resulted in a reduction of the (already low) basal SSA activity (Figure 2A), and re-expression of wt BRCA1 restored the SSA activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The BARD1-binding mutants (C61G and C64R) showed greatly reduced SSA activities.
source: As reported previously that pathogenic missense mutations in the RING domain can cause defects in both HR and SSA (Towler et al., 2013), we found that the BARD1-binding mutants (C61G and C64R) showed greatly reduced SSA activities (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B and is consistent with a previous report cited as Towler et al., 2013.

claim: All the BRCT mutants were completely defective in SSA.
source: At the same time, all the BRCT mutants were completely defective.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the SSA assay.

claim: The L1407P and M1411T mutations elevated SSA by ~2.5-fold.
source: In contrast, the three mutations that impact PALB2 binding all resulted in increased SSA activity. In particular, the L1407P and M1411T mutations elevated SSA by ~2.5-fold.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the SSA assay.

claim: BRCA1 interactions with BARD1 and BRCT-binding partners are both required for its function in the resection step of the DSB repair.
source: This finding suggests that BRCA1 interactions with BARD1 and BRCT-binding partners are both required for its function in the resection step of the DSB repair, whereas the BRCA1-PALB2 interaction functions downstream to promote HR and reduce SSA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on SSA and HR activities of various mutants.

claim: The BRCA1-PALB2 interaction functions downstream to promote HR and reduce SSA.
source: This finding suggests that BRCA1 interactions with BARD1 and BRCT-binding partners are both required for its function in the resection step of the DSB repair, whereas the BRCA1-PALB2 interaction functions downstream to promote HR and reduce SSA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on SSA and HR activities of various mutants.

claim: Loss of BRCA2 increases SSA in mouse cells.
source: It has been reported that loss of BRCA2 increases SSA in mouse cells (Stark et al., 2004; Tutt et al., 2001), and a recent report showed that some PALB2 heterozygous human lymphoblastoid cell lines have increased SSA activity (Obermeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stark et al., 2004 and Tutt et al., 2001.

claim: Some PALB2 heterozygous human lymphoblastoid cell lines have increased SSA activity.
source: It has been reported that loss of BRCA2 increases SSA in mouse cells (Stark et al., 2004; Tutt et al., 2001), and a recent report showed that some PALB2 heterozygous human lymphoblastoid cell lines have increased SSA activity (Obermeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Obermeier et al., 2016.

claim: Depletion of BRCA2 caused substantial upregulation of SSA, with BRCA2 siRNAs stimulating SSA by 1.8–5.4 fold.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, depletion of either protein caused substantial upregulation of SSA, with BRCA2 siRNAs stimulating SSA by 1.8–5.4 fold and PALB2 siRNAs 5.6–7.2 fold.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Depletion of PALB2 caused substantial upregulation of SSA, with PALB2 siRNAs stimulating SSA by 5.6–7.2 fold.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, depletion of either protein caused substantial upregulation of SSA, with BRCA2 siRNAs stimulating SSA by 1.8–5.4 fold and PALB2 siRNAs 5.6–7.2 fold.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RAD52 has been shown to possess strand annealing activity in vitro.
source: RAD52 has been shown to possess strand annealing activity in vitro (Mortensen et al., 1996) and to promote SSA in vivo (Stark et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mortensen et al., 1996.

claim: RAD52 promotes SSA in vivo.
source: RAD52 has been shown to possess strand annealing activity in vitro (Mortensen et al., 1996) and to promote SSA in vivo (Stark et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stark et al., 2004.

claim: Strong depletion of RAD52 reduced basal SSA.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, strong depletion of RAD52 (by siRNA #1972) reduced basal SSA, whereas relatively mild depletion of RAD52 (by siRNA #2569) showed little effect.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Strong RAD52 depletion greatly impeded the increase of SSA elicited by both BRCA2 and PALB2 loss.
source: Strong RAD52 depletion greatly impeded the increase of SSA elicited by both BRCA2 and PALB2 loss, while the relatively weaker depletion of RAD52 also reduced the upregulation of SSA upon loss of either BRCA2 or PALB2, albeit to lesser extents.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the SSA assay with combined knockdowns.

claim: The BRCA1- and BRCA2-binding mutants of PALB2 all showed dramatically reduced HR activity.
source: As expected, and in contrast to wt PALB2, which effectively restored HR in reporter cells depleted of the endogenous protein, the BRCA1- and BRCA2-binding mutants all showed dramatically reduced HR activity (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Re-expression of wt PALB2 in the SA-GFP reporter cells depleted of the endogenous PALB2 significantly suppressed the greatly enhanced SSA activity.
source: Re-expression of wt PALB2 in the SA-GFP reporter cells depleted of the endogenous PALB2 significantly suppressed the greatly enhanced SSA activity, whereas neither the BRCA1-binding mutants nor the BRCA2-binding mutant showed such ability (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Neither the BRCA1-binding mutants nor the BRCA2-binding mutant of PALB2 showed ability to suppress SSA.
source: Re-expression of wt PALB2 in the SA-GFP reporter cells depleted of the endogenous PALB2 significantly suppressed the greatly enhanced SSA activity, whereas neither the BRCA1-binding mutants nor the BRCA2-binding mutant showed such ability (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PALB2 controls the HR/SSA pathway choice following resection.
source: Taken together, our results establish that PALB2 controls the HR/SSA pathway choice following resection and that the interactions between PALB2 with both BRCA1 and BRCA2 are required for this function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on PALB2 mutants and their effects on HR and SSA.

claim: The interactions between PALB2 with both BRCA1 and BRCA2 are required for controlling HR/SSA pathway choice.
source: Taken together, our results establish that PALB2 controls the HR/SSA pathway choice following resection and that the interactions between PALB2 with both BRCA1 and BRCA2 are required for this function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on PALB2 mutants and their effects on HR and SSA.

claim: MDA-MB-436 cells are BRCA1-deficient, triple negative breast cancer cells.
source: To profile the functional impact and therapeutic relevance of BRCA1 variants, we developed a relatively simple drug sensitivity assay (Figure 3A–B) using the BRCA1-deficient, triple negative MDA-MB-436 breast cancer cells (Elstrodt et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Elstrodt et al., 2006.

claim: Resistance to PARPi was found to largely correlate with the HR activity of each variant.
source: Resistance to PARPi was found to largely correlate with the HR activity of each variant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from HR assay and PARPi resistance assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The BARD1-binding mutants (C61G and C64R), the PALB2-binding mutants (M1400V, M1407P and M1411T) and the BRCT mutants all demonstrated virtually no growth under PARP inhibition.
source: Specifically, the BARD1-binding mutants (C61G and C64R), the PALB2-binding mutants (M1400V, M1407P and M1411T) and the BRCT mutants all demonstrated virtually no growth under PARP inhibition, whereas other VUSs were fully or largely resistant.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the PARPi resistance assay.

claim: BRCA1-M1400V failed to confer PARPi resistance despite showing 73% of the HR activity of the wt protein.
source: Notably, BRCA1-M1400V, which showed only moderately impaired binding to PALB2 and 73% of the HR activity of the wt protein (Figure 1B,D), failed to confer PARPi resistance.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HR assay and PARPi resistance assay.

claim: The pattern of cisplatin resistance largely reflected the HR activities of the variants.
source: The pattern of cisplatin resistance also largely reflected the HR activities of the variants, as the RING, CC and BRCT mutants all showed hypersensitivity, while other variants conferred greater than ~90% colony-forming ability of the wt protein.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from HR assay and cisplatin resistance assay.

claim: HR activity, but not SSA activity, correlates with drug resistance.
source: These data clearly demonstrate the correlation between HR activity, but not SSA activity, and drug resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing HR, SSA, and drug resistance data.

claim: The RING, CC and BRCT domains and their corresponding binding partners are important for BRCA1 function in DNA repair.
source: They also underscore the importance of the RING, CC and BRCT domains and their corresponding binding partners for BRCA1 function in DNA repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on various mutants.

claim: BRCA1-C61G showed a more diffuse localization pattern than the wt protein.
source: Indeed, BRCA1-C61G, which does not bind BARD1, showed a more diffuse localization pattern than the wt protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Patient-derived mutations that truncate BRCA1 at the BRCT domain have been reported to cause BRCA1 to localize primarily in the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, patient-derived mutations that truncate BRCA1 at the BRCT domain have been reported to cause BRCA1 to localize primarily in the cytoplasm (Rodriguez et al., 2004), even though the mutants retain intact NLSs and can still bind BARD1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rodriguez et al., 2004.

claim: The localization defect of the BRCT mutants cannot be rescued by Leptomycin B (LMB).
source: The localization defect of the BRCT mutants cannot be rescued by Leptomycin B (LMB), which blocks CRM1-dependent export but can instead be rescued by co-expression of BARD1 (Rodriguez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and consistent with a previous report cited as Rodriguez et al., 2004.

claim: The localization defect of the BRCT mutants can be rescued by co-expression of BARD1.
source: The localization defect of the BRCT mutants cannot be rescued by Leptomycin B (LMB), which blocks CRM1-dependent export but can instead be rescued by co-expression of BARD1 (Rodriguez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E and consistent with a previous report cited as Rodriguez et al., 2004.

claim: The majority of the BRCT missense mutants were expressed at much lower levels than the wt protein presumably due to destabilization.
source: We consider the BRCT point mutants to be different from truncating mutants for two reasons: first, the majority of the these mutants were expressed at much lower levels than the wt protein presumably due to destabilization, whereas the truncating mutants were not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), although frameshift mutations often cause nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of mRNA in vivo; second, the missense mutants may still bind known interaction partners with low affinity or even certain unknown factors that may affect their localization.
evidence: This is based on protein expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The BRCT domain may bind a heretofore unidentified factor that promotes BRCA1 nuclear entry.
source: Collectively, the data lend strong support to the notion that the BRCT mutants may be unable to enter the nucleus and further suggest that the BRCT domain may bind a heretofore unidentified factor that promotes BRCA1 nuclear entry, with BARD1 directly or indirectly involved in the process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the localization data.

claim: Co-expression of BARD1 slightly increased the HR activity of some of the BRCT mutants, but the overall effect was modest at best.
source: Co-expression of BARD1 slightly increased the HR activity of some of the mutants, but the overall effect was modest at best (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The lack of HDR activity of the BRCT mutants is due to both their localization defect and their inability to interact with one or more binding partners.
source: These data suggest that the lack of HDR activity of the BRCT mutants is due to both their localization defect and, perhaps more importantly, their inability to interact with one or more of the three binding partners, namely Abraxas, CtIP and BRIP1, or with another binding partner yet to be identified.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on BRCT mutants.

claim: The I26A mutation was isolated in a screen for residues in the RING domain that abrogate E3 ligase activity without affecting BARD1 binding.
source: An artificial I26A mutation was isolated in a screen for residues in the RING domain that abrogate E3 ligase activity without affecting BARD1 binding (Brzovic et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brzovic et al., 2003.

claim: Mouse cells carrying a I26A knockin allele did not show any significant defect in HR activity.
source: It was first thought that the E3 ligase activity may play an important role in DNA repair and/or tumor suppression; however, mouse cells carrying a I26A knockin allele did not show any significant defect in HR activity (Reid et al., 2008), and the mutant protein was still able to suppress mammary tumor development in Brca1 conditional knockout models (Shakya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reid et al., 2008.

claim: The I26A mutant protein was still able to suppress mammary tumor development in Brca1 conditional knockout models.
source: It was first thought that the E3 ligase activity may play an important role in DNA repair and/or tumor suppression; however, mouse cells carrying a I26A knockin allele did not show any significant defect in HR activity (Reid et al., 2008), and the mutant protein was still able to suppress mammary tumor development in Brca1 conditional knockout models (Shakya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: I26A substantially reduced, by about three fold, the coIP of endogenous BARD1 with ectopically expressed BRCA1.
source: To our surprise, I26A substantially reduced, by about three fold, the coIP of endogenous BARD1 with ectopically expressed BRCA1 (Figure 5A), indicating that this mutation significantly weakens the BRCA1-BARD1 interaction.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: I26A is a complex mutation affecting at least two different BRCA1 properties.
source: Thus, I26A is a complex mutation affecting at least two different BRCA1 properties.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing I26A affects both E3 ligase activity and BARD1 binding.

claim: I26A reduced the HR activity of BRCA1 by ~30%.
source: Functionally, I26A reduced the HR activity of BRCA1 by ~30% (Figure 5B); although the apparent HR defect caused by I26A was mild, the mutation caused a 67% reduction in colony formation in the presence of cisplatin and virtually a complete loss of resistance to olaparib (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: I26A caused a 67% reduction in colony formation in the presence of cisplatin.
source: Functionally, I26A reduced the HR activity of BRCA1 by ~30% (Figure 5B); although the apparent HR defect caused by I26A was mild, the mutation caused a 67% reduction in colony formation in the presence of cisplatin and virtually a complete loss of resistance to olaparib (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: I26A caused virtually a complete loss of resistance to olaparib.
source: Functionally, I26A reduced the HR activity of BRCA1 by ~30% (Figure 5B); although the apparent HR defect caused by I26A was mild, the mutation caused a 67% reduction in colony formation in the presence of cisplatin and virtually a complete loss of resistance to olaparib (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: BRCA1 can be sumoylated and this modification promotes the E3 ligase activity of the BRCA1/BARD1 complex.

claim: There is a positive but non-linear correlation between apparent HR activity and drug resistance.

claim: The HR function of BRCA1 requires the RING, CC and BRCT domains.

claim: Conditional knock out of either Brca1 or Bard1 in murine mammary epithelial cells led to the development of mammary carcinomas that are indistinguishable from each other.
source: Conditional knock out of either Brca1 or Bard1 in murine mammary epithelial cells led to the development of mammary carcinomas that are indistinguishable from each other (Shakya et al., 2008), and the BRCA1 C61G mutant that abrogates BARD1 binding failed to suppress mammary tumor development in mice (Drost et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shakya et al., 2008.

claim: The BRCA1 C61G mutant that abrogates BARD1 binding failed to suppress mammary tumor development in mice.
source: Conditional knock out of either Brca1 or Bard1 in murine mammary epithelial cells led to the development of mammary carcinomas that are indistinguishable from each other (Shakya et al., 2008), and the BRCA1 C61G mutant that abrogates BARD1 binding failed to suppress mammary tumor development in mice (Drost et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Drost et al., 2011.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Densham et al., 2016.

claim: I26A mutant mouse cells showed reduced gene targeting efficiency and increased chromosomal abnormalities after MMC treatment.
source: At the same time, although I26A mutant mouse cells showed no defect in apparent HR activity or MMC resistance, reduced gene targeting efficiency and increased chromosomal abnormalities after MMC treatment were noted (Reid et al., 2008), indicative of a possible defect in HR in mouse cells as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reid et al., 2008.

claim: CtIP binding to BRCA1 is dispensable for CtIP-mediated DNA resection.
source: It has recently been shown that CtIP binding to BRCA1 is dispensable for CtIP-mediated DNA resection (Polato et al., 2014; Reczek et al., 2013), yet to what extent BRCA1 HR activity depends on Abraxas and BRIP1 remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Polato et al., 2014 and Reczek et al., 2013.

claim: BARD1 can significantly rescue nuclear localization of BRCT mutants but not their HR defects.
source: Our finding that BARD1 can significantly rescue nuclear localization of BRCT mutants but not their HR defects (Figure 4F) also supports an important and direct role of the BRCT domain for BRCA1 DNA repair activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: BRCA1 plays a key role in resection.
source: Consistent with early observations made in mouse cells (Stark et al., 2004), BRCA1 depletion reduced the efficiency of both HR and SSA, whereas depletion of BRCA2 led to severe loss of HR (data not shown) but increased SSA (Figure 2B). As efficient resection is necessary for both repair mechanisms, the data is consistent with the notion that BRCA1 plays a key role in resection (Bunting et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data and is consistent with a previous report cited as Bunting et al., 2010.

claim: PALB2 is the key partner of BRCA1 specifically for its HR function.
source: Based on the available data, PALB2 is the key partner of BRCA1 specifically for its HR function and the primary switch point, acting upstream of BRCA2, for HDR pathways following resection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on PALB2 and its role in HR/SSA pathway choice.

claim: PALB2 is the primary switch point, acting upstream of BRCA2, for HDR pathways following resection.
source: Based on the available data, PALB2 is the key partner of BRCA1 specifically for its HR function and the primary switch point, acting upstream of BRCA2, for HDR pathways following resection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on PALB2 and its role in HR/SSA pathway choice.

claim: Relatively common VUSs outside the RING and BRCT domains do not significantly affect the HDR activity of BRCA1.
source: Our results demonstrate that relatively common VUSs outside the RING and BRCT domains do not significantly affect the HDR activity of BRCA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on various VUSs.

claim: Olaparib has recently been approved for the treatment of BRCA1/2 mutant ovarian cancer.
source: Platinum-based therapeutics have been commonly used for treatment of ovarian cancer, and olaparib has recently been approved for the treatment of BRCA1/2 mutant ovarian cancer, with multiple trials on breast and other cancers ongoing or recently completed.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical approval status of olaparib.

claim: Platinum-based therapeutics and olaparib generate lesions that block or collapse DNA replication forks, leading to DSBs that require HR and therefore BRCA1/2 for repair.
source: These agents generate lesions that block or collapse DNA replication forks, leading to DSBs that require HR and therefore BRCA1/2 for repair (Lord and Ashworth, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lord and Ashworth, 2016.

claim: Patients with relatively common missense mutations in the RING and BRCT domains, such as C61G and A1708E, or rare mutations in the CC motif, such as L1407P or M1411T, are likely to respond to platinum- or PARPi-based therapies.
source: Based on data from this study and other recent studies, patients with relatively common missense mutations in the RING and BRCT domains, such as C61G and A1708E, respectively, or rare mutations in the CC motif, such as L1407P or M1411T, are likely to respond to platinum- or PARPi-based therapies, unless resistance mechanisms have already occurred prior to treatment or are induced by the treatment (Lord and Ashworth, 2013).
evidence: This is a clinical prediction based on the experimental data from this study.

claim: All other top 22 missense variants are fully or mostly functional both in HR and in conferring cisplatin and olaparib resistance.
source: However, except for C61G and A1708E, all other top 22 missense variants are fully or mostly functional both in HR and in conferring cisplatin and olaparib resistance (Figure 3C), which corroborates with clinical genetics evidence to further cast doubts on their pathogenicity and diminish the likelihood of a positive response of the patients to the above regimens.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: It is unlikely for any VUS outside the RING, CC and BRCT domains to be strongly pathogenic or to elicit high sensitivity to platinum or PARPi therapies.
source: Based on the results of our deletion analyses and other available data, it is unlikely for any VUS outside the RING, CC and BRCT domains to be strongly pathogenic or to elicit high sensitivity to platinum or PARPi therapies (unless it destabilizes the transcript or protein).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on deletions and VUSs.
